newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela says he has not endorsed successor - radio.
newsitem.headline: Mandela says he has not endorsed successor - radio.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela has denied endorsing his deputy Thabo Mbeki as his successor, saying it was a decision for the party, state radio reported on Sunday.

The South African Broadcasting Corporation quoted a source in the African National Congress national executive committee (NEC) saying the issue came up during an NEC meeting in Johannesburg this weekend.
"Mandela says he has not endorsed Deputy President Thabo Mbeki as his successor," the radio said.

"Mandela says democratic procedures will be followed in the election of both the ANC leader and president of the country when he steps down. He says he will leave the issue of his successor as party leader to the ANC congress, which is to be held next year," it said.
Asked about the report, NEC member Mathew Phosa told Reuters: "The issue was not on the agenda."
ANC spokesman Ronnie Mamoepa said it had always been party policy that leaders would be chosen at national congresses.
Mandela, 78, has repeatedly said he will step down as president in 1999 when general elections are due.

Last July he gave a clear signal he believed Mbeki was the best person to fill his shoes, saying in a television interview: "He is very talented and very popular and if the organisation elected him I would feel they had made the right decision."
This comment and others by Mandela led many political and economic commentators to take it as read that Mbeki had Mandela's personal backing to take over in 1999.
